options.why: Uses pyramid despite the two matching pentagonal bases.
Names the joining faces instead of the base.
Counts visible faces instead of the sides of the base.

questions.solution_text: The matching bases are pentagons, so it is a pentagonal prism.

options.why: Uses prism even though the solid has one base and an apex.
Names the triangular side faces instead of the base.
Uses a broad base description and the wrong family.

questions.solution_text: The solid has a square base and an apex, so it is a square pyramid.

questions.question_text: A prism has two matching hexagonal ends. What is its name?

options.why: Keeps the base name but ignores that there are two matching bases.
Names the joining side faces instead of the bases.
Uses informal wording and changes the solid family.

questions.solution_text: A prism is named after its base, which is a hexagon.

questions.question_text: A pyramid has $8$ triangular side faces. What is its name?

options.why: Subtracts one from the side-face count before naming the base.
Finds the base correctly but chooses the wrong solid family.
Names the side-face shape rather than the base shape.

questions.solution_text: Eight triangular side faces meet the eight sides of an octagonal base.

questions.question_text: A prism has $12$ vertices. What is its name?

options.why: Uses the total vertex count as the number of sides on one base.
Halves the vertex count and then subtracts one.
Finds six base vertices but changes the family to a pyramid.

questions.solution_text: The two bases share the $12$ vertices equally, so each is a hexagon.

questions.question_text: Which name can also describe a cube?

options.why: A cube has no apex and has two matching square bases.
A cube has square, not triangular, bases.
Uses a pyramid name for a solid with no apex.

questions.solution_text: A cube has two identical parallel square bases, so it is a square prism.
